title: High Thermal Conductivity of Back-End-of-Line Compatible Diamond Films
authors: Jinwen Liu, Chufei Cheng, Feifei Tan, Jinquan Zhang, Di Lu, Bing Dai, Jiaqi Zhu, Runsheng Wang, Zhe Cheng
abstract: Back-end-of-line (BEOL) thermal management requires electrically insulating heat-spreading dielectric that can be integrated within thermal budgets below 400 C. Here, we report polycrystalline diamond films grown directly on Si at a substrate temperature below 400C. Two films with average thickness of 760 and 1000 nm were characterized by Raman spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR). Raman spectra show a sharp diamond peak with minor signatures of non-diamond carbon, while SEM reveals lateral growth and large grain size. Temperature dependent TDTR measurements were performed from room temperature to 100C. Sensitivity analysis indicates that the sensitivity of cross-plane thermal conductivity is comparative to the in-plane thermal conductivity. Accordingly, the films were analyzed using an isotropic thermal model by considering the nearly-isotropic grain structure, yielding room temperature effective thermal conductivity of 73 and 86 W m-1 K-1, respectively. These values are about two orders of magnitude higher than those of conventional dielectric materials and demonstrate the potential of diamond films grown at low temperatures as dielectric heat-spreading layers.
summary: This paper reports on the creation and characterization of polycrystalline diamond films suitable for use as dielectric heat spreaders in advanced semiconductor packaging (BEOL). Using TDTR measurements, the authors determined that these low-temperature grown films exhibit extremely high thermal conductivities, demonstrating their potential to improve thermal management in microelectronic devices.
main_problem: Developing thermally conductive dielectric materials for Back-End-of-Line (BEOL) thermal management that can operate within low temperature budgets (<400°C).
main_result: The authors successfully fabricated polycrystalline diamond films with effective room temperature thermal conductivities of 73 and 86 W m-1 K-1, which are significantly higher than conventional dielectrics.
method: Characterization involved Raman spectroscopy to check crystal quality, SEM for morphology, and Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements to quantify thermal conductivity.
model_or_system: The physical system is polycrystalline diamond films grown directly on an Si substrate at low temperatures. The analysis models the heat transport using an isotropic model due to the nearly-isotropic grain structure observed.
key_observables: Room temperature effective thermal conductivities ($\sim 73$ and $\sim 86 	ext{ W m}^{-1} 	ext{ K}^{-1}$), sharp diamond Raman peaks, and large grain sizes visible via SEM.
important_parameters: Low growth temperature (<400°C), film thicknesses (760 nm and 1000 nm), and the comparison to conventional dielectric materials' thermal conductivity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an isotropic thermal model ($\kappa_r = \kappa_z$) because sensitivity analysis showed comparable in-plane and cross-plane heat transport sensitivities.
figures_summary: Figures show TDTR measurement setups, Raman spectra confirming diamond purity, and SEM images illustrating the large grain size of the films.
paper_structure: The paper follows a standard experimental structure: introducing the thermal management problem in BEOL, detailing characterization methods (Raman, SEM, TDTR), presenting results showing high conductivity values, and concluding with the potential application of these low-temperature grown diamond layers.
why_interesting: While focused on materials science/thermal engineering, the study's quantitative measurement of phonon transport in crystalline solids is relevant to understanding thermal properties in complex quantum systems or interfaces where heat dissipation is critical.
